text: I’ll model a 1/28 annular sector from one blade centre-plane to the next, subtracting the two adjacent half-blades. This makes the passage walls the pressure side of one blade and suction side of its neighbour; the remaining portions of the two radial sector planes are the separate periodic patches. Because camber magnitude and location were not specified, I’ll assume a NACA-style mean line with 2% camber at 40% chord (a NACA 2406 section). I’ll first inspect the root/tip sections in an unwrapped axial–tangential view. The eventual mesh will be an unstructured Gmsh tetrahedral mesh imported into OpenFOAM, coarse first, with radial refinement through the 45 mm span.

The section construction is numerically correct, but the first plot mixed metres and millimetres on equal-aspect axes, making the profile visually collapse. I’ll now inspect the installed build123d loft and primitive APIs before constructing the annular sector and twisted blade solids.

The installed kernel supports direct algebra-mode lofting. I’ll construct an exact annular-sector face from two circular arcs and extrude it axially, then loft each adjacent blade through several radial sections so the stated linear twist is represented smoothly. This next step only builds and measures the CAD solids; meshing follows after the coarse CAD view is checked.

I’ll now create the two full neighbouring twisted blades in metres. Their centres lie on the two sector planes at ±half-pitch, so intersecting/subtracting them from the sector leaves exactly the requested pressure wall on one side and suction wall on the other. Seven radial loft sections are used for the 35° linear twist.

The first loft is invalid because I wrapped each section around a cylinder, making its supposedly radial cross-section slightly non-planar. That is not appropriate for a blade section. I’ll correct it to a planar section in the local axial–tangential plane at each radius, then re-check validity and dimensions.
The correction had a Python tuple-construction typo before any shape was rebound. I’ll rerun only the corrected planar-section loft.

The corrected lofts are valid. I’ll build the exact hub-to-shroud sector face next and inspect its edge endpoints before extrusion, ensuring the two periodic planes really are separated by one 12.857° pitch rather than relying on a bounding-box classification.

I’ll now extrude that exact annular face between the inlet and outlet planes and subtract both adjacent blade solids. The resulting coarse CAD fluid volume will be exported as a metre-declared STEP and rendered before any mesh is generated.
The sector face is valid; the installed extrude API requires a separate scalar amount even when a direction is supplied. I’ll rerun that single construction with `amount=AXIAL_LENGTH`.

The fluid solid itself is valid and single-volume. Export failed only because this build123d version names the metre unit differently; I’ll inspect the available unit enum before repeating the successful construction/export in an accepted cell.
I’ll now repeat the valid fluid construction and export it with `Unit.M`, preserving metre scale explicitly.

The coarse CAD volume is now valid and exported. I’ll render the tessellated fluid boundary from an oblique view, with axes in metres, to visually confirm the annular wedge, inlet/outlet extensions, and blade-side cutouts.
Understood. I’ll stop iterating on CAD presentation and import the existing valid STEP directly into Gmsh now, inspect only the surface entity list needed to assign patches, then mesh immediately.

The STEP imported as one valid volume at the correct metre scale. Its lofted blade skins are split into many narrow B-spline faces, but this does not prevent meshing. I’ll assign patches by analytic surface provenance: exact inlet/outlet planes, exact hub/shroud cylinders, exact ±half-pitch planes, and the remaining blade-skin faces split by which neighbouring blade they came from. Then I’ll generate the coarse tetrahedral mesh and write `passage.msh`.

The analytic classification is now clear: four planar periodic pieces (upstream/downstream portions grouped by side), two end planes, two cylinders, and the remaining B-spline blade skins. The small planar blade-root imprint is part of the hub patch. I’ll mesh at a deliberately coarse 4 mm target size and convert it to OpenFOAM immediately.

Gmsh reached 7,089 surface nodes but rejected two nearly coincident tip facets (0.049° apart). This comes from ending the loft exactly on the shroud before the Boolean cut. I’ll fix it in the mesh geometry by extending the cutting blades 1 mm beyond hub and tip while clamping the requested root/tip section angles; the retained fluid remains exactly 45–90 mm radius. Then I’ll remesh with the same coarse size.
I’ll now re-import the cleaned passage, assign all eight requested surface groups, generate the 4 mm coarse tetrahedral mesh, convert it, and run `checkMesh` in this one focused meshing step.

The cleaned Boolean is topologically valid, but the 121-point section creates hundreds of tiny loft edges; Gmsh’s surface mesher now fails on an edge intersection at the shroud. For the requested coarsest mesh, I’ll reduce the CAD section sampling to 31 cosine-spaced points and five radial loft stations. This preserves chord, 6% thickness, camber law, root stagger, and tip twist while removing sub-mesh-scale edges.

The face count reveals that the coarse blade cutters were not retained in the Boolean—the result is just the six-face empty sector—so I will not mesh that incorrect shape. I’ll inspect only cutter validity and overlap volume to correct this immediately.

The cutters are valid and spatially appear near the sector, so I’ll compare exact sector and cutter bounds/centres; this should expose whether the annular sector was translated along the wrong local axis during algebra-mode placement.

The extended coarse loft has a valid but pathological correspondence between sparse section vertices, producing no Boolean overlap despite overlapping bounds. I’ll revert radial section stations to the exact seven requested radii while keeping only the reduced 31-point profile; this is the smallest controlled change and directly tests the cutter overlap before meshing.

The overlap test shows the centre-plane interpretation is wrong for a staggered blade: one neighbour’s full chord lies outside that angular sector. I’ll switch to the standard single-passage periodic topology: one complete blade centred in a sector bounded by mid-pitch periodic planes. Its two exposed skins physically represent the pressure side of one blade and suction side of the periodic neighbour. This preserves all requested boundaries and avoids half-blade Boolean degeneracies.

The requested solidity is slightly above one at the root, so a constant-angle mid-pitch plane necessarily intersects the staggered chord. For a coarse, existing mesh I’ll proceed with the standard periodic sector and retain the blade portions inside it; the blade skins are classified pressure/suction from their position relative to the NACA mean line. I’ll mesh this now and explicitly report this topology limitation rather than delaying further.

The coarse Gmsh mesh now exists (1,781 nodes, 9,615 total elements). Conversion failed because Gmsh wrote its default MSH 4 format; this OpenFOAM converter expects legacy MSH 2.2. I’ll rewrite the existing mesh as 2.2, convert, and run `checkMesh`.
Conversion is now reading the mesh correctly; it only requires a minimal OpenFOAM `system/controlDict` to identify the case. I’ll add that mesh-only case metadata, reconvert, and check.

The OpenFOAM mesh was created with 5,969 tetrahedra and all eight named patches, but 2,960 boundary faces were placed into `defaultFaces`, indicating Gmsh 2.2 omitted physical tags for some split CAD faces. `checkMesh` then stopped while reading the resulting boundary. I’ll inspect the exact fatal message and patch table before repairing the missing physical-surface coverage.

The mesh coverage is actually complete: the “undefined” faces were subsequently assigned across the eight physical patches, and no `defaultFaces` patch remains. `checkMesh` stopped only because this OpenFOAM version loads `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` even for mesh checking. I’ll add empty mesh-only dictionaries, rerun the full check, and render the resulting mesh surface.

The mesh is closed, single-region, and has all eight patches, but the coarse Delaunay tetrahedra fail four quality checks around narrow blade/periodic intersections (max skewness 16.3). I’ll remesh the same CAD with Gmsh’s HXT tetrahedral algorithm, a 1–3 mm size range, and Netgen optimization to address those quality failures before accepting it.

HXT confirms the failure is geometric rather than algorithmic: a 51.7 µm blade/periodic intersection creates near-zero-volume cells. Blade-row circumferential phase is unspecified and arbitrary, so I’ll rotate the blade row by 2° relative to the fixed sector planes. This preserves 28-fold spacing and every blade dimension while moving the periodic cuts away from tangencies; then I’ll remesh.

A 2° phase doubles the smallest CAD edge to 0.117 mm but remains too small relative to a coarse mesh. I’ll test the phase choice numerically over a few angles and select the one maximizing the minimum retained edge, without changing the blade geometry itself.
